title: UNKNOT: project overview
subtitle: How many backgrounds can we detect? Built blind, maximum entropy, the experimental design (two paths), and the mk1 results
author: Nathan Herling
description: UNKNOT asks how many sources make up the MSVtx background, using background data only and stating a confidence for every answer. The deck covers how it was designed blind to the rank-K study and the ATLAS paper, the maximum-entropy assumption and what it gains and loses (with real mk1 phase-1 fits), the experimental design (path 1: count up to four sources; path 2: bias search in the ABCD plane), and the mk1 results: endcap one background drifting with activity, barrel one candidate split by position. Slides after 'End of vetted work' are working material. Internal, exploratory.
notes: UNKNOT: UNsupervised K-source Number and Origin Test. Research question: how many backgrounds can we detect in the MSVtx background? Two methods. Method 1, mk1 (structure): smooth curve per feature, a mix of 1 to 4 sources, the data chooses the number; a count stands only when four independent tests agree. The run is complete and frozen. Method 2, mk2 (ABCD-plane bias): read those sources through the two network scores and split the bias into dependence inside each source and dependence from mixing, reported against cut with errors. Not started. Constraint: every answer carries a stated confidence; background data only. Internal and exploratory.

Before the design. I designed this experiment without looking at Laura's rank-K work (L. Bruce, 'Rank-K ABCD in pictures', internal, 23 Oct 2026) or the ATLAS paper (Phys. Lett. B 878 (2026) 140509). Timeline: 23 Oct rank-K is built on a toy; early November only the question reached me, to model the three background sources separately; 10 to 12 Nov UNKNOT was designed and run on the real background with both references unopened; 13 Nov the results were written down and locked; only then were the references opened, for comparison. Double blind here means two independent constructions: UNKNOT never saw rank-K or the paper, and rank-K predates UNKNOT. It is not blind to the question, the three suspected sources, the group's ABCD method or the shared data files.

The principle of maximum entropy, formulated by physicist Edwin T. Jaynes in 1957: when estimating a probability distribution from partial information, choose the distribution with the highest entropy among all those that satisfy your known constraints. For UNKNOT this is an assumption, not a requirement: inside each source, each feature follows the maximum-entropy curve for a few measured averages. What we gain: smooth unbinned curves, stability at small N, a likelihood for comparing 1 to 4 sources, one detail dial set on held-out events. What we lose: spikes and placeholders such as NN1 = 0, hard edges, structure finer than the averages taken, and if detail is too low the mixture adds sources to absorb misfit. The entropy itself comes from information theory: Shannon's H = minus the sum of p log p, the uncertainty of a distribution; for a smooth curve it becomes minus the integral of f ln f. The two figures are real mk1 phase-1 output. Barrel |z|, 1,089 events: on held-out events (5-fold) the smooth curve beats a 40-bin histogram from M = 4 on, and mk1 keeps M = 6, the simplest setting within one standard error of the best. Endcap cluster time: 35% of events sit at the placeholder value -1, which a smooth curve cannot hold, so mk1 sets that spike aside and fits the other 65%; there the held-out score keeps improving up to M = 20, the top of the grid.

Experimental design. Start: what maximum entropy gives us from phase 1, per region: one smooth curve per feature with its detail M chosen on held-out events, a likelihood for scoring any event under any curve, and flags that set aside spikes and placeholders and drop dead features. Barrel: 1,089 vertices, 168 usable features; endcap: 34,970 vertices, 214 usable features. What it does not give: how the features combine. Path 1 (mk1): count the sources. Assume a mix of up to four sources, K = 1 to 4; inside a source features are independent so their curves multiply; fit each K and let four independent gates decide. Output: K with a stated confidence, plus each source's share and shape. Status: run and frozen; endcap one background drifting with activity, barrel one candidate split by position. Path 2 (mk1): bias search in the ABCD plane. Add NN1 and NN2, split ABCD non-closure into dependence inside each source and dependence created by mixing, and follow it as the cuts move. Output: bias against cut per source with errors. Not started. Both paths: background only, every answer a statistical test with a stated confidence, built blind to the rank-K study and the ATLAS paper. Footer, what a likelihood is: the height of a model's curve at an event, how probable the model says that event is; adding the logs over all events gives one number for how well the model explains the data. It gives one common score for comparing models, 1 source against 2, a curve against a histogram, one detail setting against another, always measured on events the fit never saw. What path 1 tells us and with what confidence: endcap, one background drifting with activity, since at fixed activity a smooth trend does as well as groups (z = -1.3); barrel, one candidate split by position, 56/44, passing all four gates (30 of 30 re-draws, z = 9.1), with acceptance not yet ruled out. Path 2 would tell us how much of the ABCD bias comes from mixing versus inside each source, cut by cut, with resampling errors; it has not been run, so there is no confidence to state yet.

Results. Endcap: one background whose shape drifts with activity; the apparent groups dissolve once activity is known. Barrel: one candidate split by position that holds through every gate so far; detector acceptance is not yet ruled out. Direction hints at cosmics or halo in the barrel; missing-momentum pointing marks collision debris in the endcap.
End of vetted work. Everything up to here has been reviewed for this overview. The slides that follow are working material carried over from the mk1 deck and have not yet been re-vetted.

The idea. Three suspects can each leave displaced vertices: collision debris (punch-through jets), beam-induced background, and cosmic rays. Why it matters: mixing sources with different shapes creates a correlation between the two network scores even when no single source has one, which is enough to break ABCD closure. Ground rules: background only, signal only as an acceptance reference, built blind to the rank-K study and the ATLAS paper, results frozen before comparison.

Maximum entropy: of all curves that reproduce a few measured averages, take the one that assumes nothing else. Each feature gets one smooth curve per source; features multiply inside a source; sources mix over K. Left column: what this design is good at. Right column: what it misses or fakes. Spikes, hard edges, correlation inside one source, and drift in an unsupplied variable can each fake an extra group, which is why the gates exist. The feature strip stays empty until make_feature_panels.py is run on the mk1 background file.

Pipeline. Counting lane: background file, health check and barrel/endcap split, feature sets, MaxEnt curves, mixture over K = 1-4, four gates, count. Two assumptions are flagged: each curve is smooth (A1) and features are independent inside a source (A2). Fingerprint lane: direction against detector acceptance and vertex-to-missing-momentum pointing, used to name a group only after it is counted.

One worked example: barrel, position features. G1 both scorecards pick 2; G2 the gain beats scrambled events; G3 the count holds in 30 of 30 halves and both run periods; G4 groups beat a single smooth trend at z = 9.1. Verdict: 2 groups, a candidate. Still open: the same check at fixed activity and on signal as an acceptance control. Two endcap counts stopped: timing at G1 (scorecards disagree) and activity at G4 (a smooth trend does as well, z = -1.3).
